bill.title: To amend the Congressional Accountability Act of 1995 to provide enhanced enforcement authority for occupational safety and health protections applicable to the legislative branch, to provide whistleblower protections and other antidiscrimination protections for employees of the legislative branch, and for other purposes.
bill.latestActionText: Referred to the Committee on House Administration, and in addition to the Committees on Education and Workforce, and the Judiciary, for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker, in each case for consideration of such provisions as fall within the jurisdiction of the committee concerned.

classification.plainSummary: This bill would strengthen workplace safety and health enforcement for legislative branch employees, including those working in Congress. It would add whistleblower protections and anti-discrimination safeguards for people employed by the legislative branch. The measure amends the Congressional Accountability Act of 1995 to expand these protections.

industries.rationale: Enhanced workplace safety enforcement and whistleblower protections directly affect the interests of unions representing legislative branch employees.

plain.whatItDoes: No one has written a summary of this bill yet. All we have is its title, and a title is not a description of a law. To find out what it does, you have to open the bill itself.
plain.whoItTouches: We cannot tell from the labels on this bill who it reaches. The subject is too broad to say.
plain.everydayEffect: Nothing has changed yet. The title alone does not say what would change for you, and this tool will not guess. Most bills never become law.
plain.source: From the bill title, and from the subject labels that library staff put on it. There is no official summary of this bill yet.

method.formula: score = Σ_industries ( donorShare(industry) × billWeight(industry) ), where billWeight = classifierConfidence / Σ classifierConfidence. Range 0–1, read as a weighted share of disclosed itemized money.

ordinary.text: They wrote this bill. Sponsoring a bill about your own district's industry is the ordinary case, not the odd one.
This member reported only $13,000 in total. With a small total, one ordinary donation produces a large percentage.

disclaimer: This tool places two public records next to each other: who donated to a member of Congress, and what that member legislated on. Any overlap you see is a correlation, not causation. It is not evidence of a quid pro quo, of influence, or of wrongdoing. Legislators routinely receive support from industries in their district for the same reason they legislate on them: those industries are there.
